newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to crack down on money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to crack down on money laundering.

text.p: Mexico is imposing tough new rules to prevent drug traffickers and other criminals from laundering money in the country's financial institutions, a top official said on Friday.

Giving the outline of the new measures, Federal Fiscal Prosecutor Ismael Gomez Gordillo told reporters during the annual Mexican Banking Convention in this Caribbean resort that banks would have to report suspicious or large transactions for investigation.
U.S. officials have charged that millions of dollars of drug proceeds are laundered every year through Mexican financial institutions, particularly exchange houses.

Pressure on Mexico to produce results in the drug war has grown in recent days following strong U.S. congressional opposition to President Bill Clinton's decision on Feb. 28 to recertify Mexico as an ally in the drug war.
Many congressmen in Washington believe Mexico is too corrupt to deserve full recertification and needs to be taught a lesson.

Gomez said a first set of rules would cover banks, finance houses, brokerages and exchange houses while other rules would be set for insurance companies and other institutions which were supposedly at lower risk of being used to launder money.
Full details of the regulations would be given next week, he said.
When the rules come into force at the start of May, Gomez explained, financial institutions would have to report voluntarily any operations they considered suspicious.

By Sept. 1, banks would have to draw up an internal anti-laundering manual for approval by the Finance Ministry and once this had been officially endorsed they would be obliged to report any suspicious transaction.
In addition, all transactions worth $10,000 or more in cash, foreign currency, travelers' checks, gold or silver would have to be reported from Jan. 1, 1998, he added.

Gomez said the rules would be applied equally to stop money being laundered by any criminal, not just by drug traffickers. Other targets could include kidnappers, arms traffickers, organ traffickers and organised criminals, he said.
He told reporters that no Mexican financial institution or its staff were currently under investigation for money laundering.
